- When sentiment is consistently negative or neutral over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or shift mean downward.
- After sharp spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model often overshoots and fails to correct — cap upward momentum after peak, allow for lagged mean reversion.
- In high-bearish event context (net supply > -10), model frequently overpredicts recovery; apply downward bias to 30d forecast mean, especially if sentiment is weak.
- If sentiment history shows repeated bullish/bearish alternation, model may misread trend direction — align forecast with sentiment polarity shift, not just magnitude.
- In low-event or low-sentiment periods, model tends to underestimate volatility — increase forecast variance or add small downward drift to avoid overconfidence.
- When supply net is negative and bullish events are low, model often overestimates price resilience — reduce forecast by 2–5% relative to historical mean of similar context.
- If recent true outcomes show mean reversion after high volatility, model should not assume continuation — apply smoothing or decay factor to forecast path.
